item.title: Google Photos Takeout JSON files: what to keep before fixing dates
item.description:
Google Photos Takeout JSON files: what to keep before fixing dates

Keep the JSON files while you check the export

Do not discard the JSON files just because your photos open without them. A viewable picture and a well-described picture are different preservation goals. Before tidying a Google Photos Takeout export, keep an untouched copy of the downloaded archives, retain the extracted folder structure, and investigate a small working sample.

This guide addresses one specific problem: an export contains unfamiliar JSON files, and old photos appear under a recent date. The aim is to decide what needs investigation before renaming, importing or rewriting anything—not to promise a one-click metadata repair.

Your useful output: a short record for three items showing which date you actually inspected, where companion information lives, and what remains unresolved. The blank worksheet is free to download; no account or upload is needed.

Separate three kinds of information

Google’s download documentation distinguishes a timestamp assigned by the operating system during download from original timestamps inside the media. It also says additional information, such as Google Photos comments, is exported into secondary JSON files. That is not a claim that every exported image has every field you expect.

These are different evidence sources, not three values that must always agree.
LayerWhat you are looking atQuestion to ask
File-system dateA field such as file creation or modification time in your file manager.Am I seeing a file operation date rather than the photograph’s capture date?
Embedded media metadataFields read from inside the image or video, if present.Which exact field is this viewer showing, and does it actually describe capture?
Companion informationSeparate JSON data associated with the export.Does this contain context I need to preserve, and can I establish what it describes?

A column simply called “Date” is too ambiguous for a repair decision. Record its full label and the application. An absent field means not found in this inspection; it does not prove the picture was taken on the download date. Likewise, an old date in a filename is a clue, not independent proof of capture time.

Set up a working sample without flattening the archive

Google notes that a large export can arrive in several archives. Confirm that you have downloaded the parts listed for your export before treating a missing item as lost. Recent library changes may also fall outside an export’s contents. Record the export request and download dates so you know which snapshot you are reviewing.

  1. Preserve the delivery. Keep the downloaded archive files unchanged. Do not rename or delete their contents as your first organizing step.
  2. Separate extraction from experiments. Extract into a fresh, clearly named location. If a file conflict or overwrite prompt appears, stop and investigate instead of choosing “replace all.”
  3. Copy a small working set. Choose an older camera photo, a screenshot or edited image, and a video. Keep their relative folders and candidate JSON files together. These cases can reveal different gaps.
  4. Write down what you copied. Record the original relative path and archive part. Do not merge everything into a single folder: repeated filenames would become harder to distinguish.
My photo-export review/
  downloads-kept-unchanged/
  extracted-kept-unchanged/
  working-sample/
  review-notes.txt

This is KYD’s suggested local arrangement, not a representation of Google’s archive structure. Three folders on one drive do not make three independent backups. Use the capacity guide to allow for archives, extracted files and working copies, and keep a separate recovery copy where appropriate.

Worked example: one “wrong date,” three different decisions

Invented observations for teaching—not a test of a real Google account: someone downloaded an export on October 8, 2026. Their file manager shows that day for all three sample files. They then inspect the media and candidate companion data without changing either.

Fictional review record. Identifiers A, B and C are worksheet labels, not Takeout filenames or JSON field names.
SampleAdditional observationDecision
A · Camera photoThe viewer’s capture-date field shows August 14, 2019. The picture opens correctly.No evidence yet that its embedded capture date needs repair. Check the file manager’s sorting field first.
B · ScreenshotNo capture-date field is exposed by this viewer. A candidate JSON file contains a date, but its association with B is uncertain.Leave the date unresolved. Do not write a guessed timestamp into the image.
C · VideoPlayback works. Companion information contains a description the owner wants, but the destination app does not display it in the sample import.Keep that companion data and record the import limitation. Playback alone did not preserve all desired context.

The three files look identical under one file-manager date column, but they call for three different actions. A bulk command that assigns that column’s date to every media file would erase the distinction the review just uncovered.

In this example, one item needs no demonstrated capture-date repair, one remains unresolved, and one needs a context-preservation decision. None of those outcomes authorizes deleting the source library.

Inspect one item without rewriting it

  1. Open the media itself. Use a trusted local viewer and its information panel. Note the complete field label, value and application version. If the viewer exposes no suitable field, record “not shown” instead of inventing a date.
  2. Inspect candidate JSON as text. Use a local plain-text viewer without saving changes. Do not upload family photos or metadata to an unknown online “fixer.” Names, descriptions and location-related fields may be private.
  3. Establish the association. Keep the original path, compare identifying information that is actually present, and consult documentation for the specific export or importer. A similar basename alone is not enough when several files share it. Do not assume every JSON file describes one photo.
  4. Test the destination with copies. If you intend to use a photo organizer, import only the sample into a separate test library where possible. Compare the displayed dates and wanted descriptions. Ask whether the importer supports this companion format; the presence of a JSON file does not establish support.
  5. Write a bounded conclusion. For example: “Photo opens; capture date displayed; description not imported; original export retained.” This is more useful than “metadata fixed.”

If two displays disagree, preserve both values and their labels. A different timezone display is one possibility, not an automatic diagnosis. Do not apply a library-wide time offset until you know what each field and application represents.

When a cleanup or repair should stop

  • Several possible companions: preserve them and mark the association unresolved. A rename based on a guess can make a later match harder.
  • Unreadable archive or extraction error: resolve that problem before reviewing metadata. A partial extraction is not a trustworthy inventory.
  • An importer skips context: keep the original media and companion data even if you create a convenient browsing copy elsewhere.
  • A proposed repair overwrites originals: do not run it on your only export. First understand which fields it writes and test reversible copies.

The Library of Congress’s personal-archiving guidance emphasizes keeping descriptions with photographs. The practical point here is not to preserve a particular file extension for its own sake: preserve the information you would otherwise lose about the image.

A metadata edit may change a file’s bytes even if its visible picture does not change. Use our local file copy checker on an untouched source and a plain copy when the question is copy integrity; its limit is 32 MiB per file. It does not interpret JSON, determine a correct date, or verify an importer. See how to interpret a mismatch before labelling an edited derivative corrupt.

Keep a review record you can use later

Three-item export review

Export request / download dates: ____________________

Archive parts listed / downloaded: ____________________

Untouched copy location: ____________________

For each sample: relative path · media opens? · date field label and value · candidate companion path · association confirmed or unresolved · wanted context · sample import result · next action.

Remaining unknowns: ____________________

Download the blank text worksheet

The worksheet is an original KYD template, not a Google export parser or a certificate. You may save, adapt and print it for your own archive. Fill it out locally; this website does not receive your notes. Keep completed records private and never include passwords or recovery codes.

Done for this session means: the delivered archives are retained, each inspected field is identified, ambiguous associations stay unresolved, and the next action is written down. Before relying on the export as a recovery copy, continue with the non-destructive recovery drill. Do not delete originals merely because three samples passed.

item.title: Before deleting photos: separate sync from an independent copy
item.description:
Before deleting photos: separate sync from an independent copy

The question is not “Can I see the photo?”

A thumbnail is a useful starting point, not a recovery plan. The practical question is: if this phone disappeared, could I obtain a usable copy without it? A second question matters just as much: would that copy survive an accidental deletion in the app I use every day?

This guide uses a copy map to answer those questions. It is for personal photo libraries, not forensic recovery or business retention. Stop before deletion if the only available copy is on a failing device; repeated attempts to organize or rewrite it can make a recovery situation harder.

Start by choosing one small, non-sensitive sample: an older photo, a recent photo and a video. Do not delete those samples as a test. Their job is to reveal gaps before you change your library.

Draw the copy map before choosing a cleanup button

PhoneDaily photo library
↔Sync
Cloud libraryAccount-dependent
→Export
Separate copyOutside that sync

Label locations, not devices. Two folders on one laptop share that laptop’s failure risk. Two devices signed into the same synchronized library can share deletion behavior. A drive containing a deliberate export is a separate branch only if your synchronization or backup rules do not remove it when the working library changes.

Write down a simple test for each arrow: “Will a deletion here change the destination?” If you cannot answer from the service documentation and your settings, label the destination unknown. Do not count it as an independent copy yet.

Three actions that sound similar but do different things

Service behavior checked October 7, 2026. Check the actual confirmation screen before acting.
ActionWhat the provider describesWhat to verify first
Delete in iCloud PhotosDeletion is reflected across devices using iCloud Photos.An independent export, not just another synchronized device.
Delete in Google PhotosThe app’s delete action can remove the device copy and backed-up copies across devices with backup enabled.Whether you intend to remove the cloud item, not merely free phone space.
Google Photos “Free up space” on AndroidRemoves backed-up device copies. Cloud access remains, but those removed local files are not available offline in the device gallery.Completed backup, correct account, and which files you still need offline.

These are different operations, not interchangeable instructions. Apple’s Optimize Storage keeps smaller device versions as needed while originals remain in iCloud. That helps device capacity but is not a separate archive. The official links below explain the service details; menus vary by app and OS version.

Worked example: a reassuring count that hides a gap

Hypothetical case: a family sees 8,400 items on the phone and 8,400 in the cloud. The matching total does not establish that all 8,400 are the same items, that videos play, or that an export contains the wanted originals. One omitted video and one duplicate image could leave the count unchanged.

  1. Check a recent photo that should have uploaded after the last trip.
  2. Check an old photo from a folder that was imported rather than captured by this phone.
  3. Export a video, then play its beginning, middle and end from the export.
  4. Record where the exported samples were opened and whether that location participates in sync.

If the imported folder is absent, the appropriate next task is to identify the missing scope—not to delete until counts happen to match. Google Photos exposes backup status and folder settings; those are useful checks, but the sample still needs to match the library you intend to preserve.

Leave with evidence, not a green badge

For each important group, record a location, the format you need, the export date and a successful opening check. Do not put account identifiers or private filenames into public support reports. A sample is deliberately limited: it can expose a problem, but cannot prove every item is recoverable.

Use the photo backup self-check to turn missing evidence into a next-action list. Then follow the non-destructive recovery drill. Neither tool grants permission to erase the source. Keep originals until you understand the remaining risks and have verified the copies you need.

Sources & scope

Source pages checked October 7, 2026. Provider behavior is source-based; examples and the planning method are KYD’s own synthesis, not a hands-on cloud-service test.

  • Apple: how iCloud Photos handles originals and deletions
  • Google Photos: deleting photos and videos
  • Google Photos: free up space on an Android device
  • Google Photos: backup status and device folders

item.title: How to verify a copied photo file—and understand a mismatch
item.description:
How to verify a copied photo file—and understand a mismatch

A copy check answers one narrow question

Two files can show the same photograph without containing the same bytes. One might be a resized JPEG, the other an original HEIC. Conversely, two byte-identical copies can both contain a damaged original. Decide which question you want to answer before choosing a test.

The KYD file copy checker answers: are these two selected files byte-for-byte identical? It reads them locally, compares every byte and displays a SHA-256 fingerprint for each. It does not upload, decode, repair or delete them. It does not scan a folder, inspect your cloud account or authenticate the person who created a file.

A small, repeatable comparison

  1. Keep the source untouched. Copy it to a different location using your normal file-copy method.
  2. Wait for the copy operation to finish. Make sure both are actual downloaded files rather than cloud placeholders.
  3. Select the source as File A and the copied file as File B in the checker. The tool accepts files up to 32 MiB each.
  4. Run the comparison. Record the result and the two fingerprints locally if needed.
  5. Open the copied image in a trusted viewer. For a video, also check playback and audio. A byte comparison is not a media-decoding test.

The file picker only grants this page access to the files you choose. Cloud-backed file pickers may themselves download a file through the operating system before the browser can read it. That is different from this tool uploading anything. If you need to avoid that download, choose files already saved locally.

Interpret the result without jumping to a conclusion

ResultWhat it establishesNext step
Byte-identicalThe selected contents match at the time of reading. Names and timestamps are not compared.Open the copy. Keep checking the rest of the collection and independence of storage.
Different byte sizesThese are not identical copies.Check whether you selected an original versus an export, edit or thumbnail.
Same size, different bytesSize alone would have missed the difference.Compare export settings and repeat a plain copy into a new folder.
Unable to read / too largeNo comparison was completed.Leave the originals alone. Use an appropriate trusted desktop verification tool for larger files.

Google Photos Storage saver can compress or change a file’s format. Apple also distinguishes exporting originals from other ways of saving photos. A mismatch after conversion is not, by itself, evidence of corruption. If your goal is to preserve the camera original, compare unmodified originals rather than a rendered edit. Keep a useful edited version as an additional item if you want both.

Try a known result before selecting personal files

The checker has a built-in demonstration using three tiny text byte sequences, not photos. It compares abc with another abc, then with abd. The first pair must match. The second pair must differ even though both files are three bytes long.

The expected SHA-256 for the UTF-8 bytes of abc, with no newline, is:

ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad

This fixture catches a particularly bad implementation: declaring two files equal because their names or sizes match. KYD’s direct comparison checks contents; the fingerprint is also useful as a record you can compare later. A fingerprint has no built-in proof of origin—an untrusted file accompanied by an untrusted fingerprint is still untrusted.

Where this check stops

One match does not inventory a whole library, preserve album membership or confirm account recovery. Live or motion photos can involve more than a single still-image file; companion media and metadata need their own checks. Do not treat selecting one exported JPEG as a test of every component.

The browser digest API reads whole inputs into memory, so this implementation caps each file at 32 MiB. It deliberately avoids promising multi-gigabyte video verification. For a collection, maintain a manifest and use a suitable batch verification workflow; do not laboriously rename hundreds of originals to fit a two-file tool.

After a successful copy comparison, test the broader recovery path using the recovery drill. A copy that cannot be found, opened or accessed without a lost device is not yet a useful recovery plan.

item.title: Plan photo backup space from your own library—not a photo-count estimate
item.description:
Plan photo backup space from your own library—not a photo-count estimate

Measure the files you intend to preserve

“Ten thousand photos” is not a capacity measurement. The space needed by ten thousand small screenshots is different from that of a mixed library containing RAW photographs and long videos. Start with the byte size of the files you actually plan to copy.

This planner budgets a new, full copy on one destination. It is not a subscription recommendation or a prediction of phone storage. If a destination already contains part of the same archive, do not blindly add the full library again: first establish what exists and what your backup software will retain. Do not delete that existing copy to make the estimate fit.

Use exported-file sizes where possible. Optimized phone storage or a compressed cloud collection may not represent the size of the originals you want to keep. Export a manageable sample, check its format, then measure the actual collection when feasible.

Make the assumptions visible

Future archive = current archive + monthly growth × months + extra retained versions
Space budget = future archive ÷ (1 − reserve fraction)

Reserve is a chosen planning allowance, not a manufacturer requirement. In this model it is a fraction of the total allocated space budget. A 20% reserve therefore means dividing by 0.8, not simply adding 20% to the data amount.

“Extra retained versions” means additional old or changed files kept alongside the current archive. Enter zero if you are planning only one full version, but recognize that doing so does not budget version history. Software that retains multiple full snapshots could need much more space; this simple model does not simulate deduplication or compression.

Worked case: 120 GB today, a year of growth

Hypothetical inputs, not a measured user library: 120 GB current archive, 4 GB of net additions per month, 12 months, 30 GB of extra retained versions, and a 20% reserve.

  1. Growth: 4 × 12 = 48 GB.
  2. Future archive plus versions: 120 + 48 + 30 = 198 GB.
  3. Total budget: 198 ÷ 0.8 = 247.5 GB.
  4. If the intended destination reports 200 GB of free space, the gap is 47.5 GB.

The answer is not “buy the next advertised size.” Compare with usable free space after formatting and other stored files. If you intend two independent destinations, each needs its own suitable budget; two copies competing for the same free space do not create two independent devices.

Run these numbers in the backup space planner. It also doubles only your growth assumption for a sensitivity check: 120 + 8 × 12 + 30 = 246 GB of data, requiring 307.5 GB with the same reserve. The 60 GB difference shows why a small change in monthly capture habits can matter more than rounding a current reading.

Keep GB and GiB separate

This tool uses decimal GB: 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. A GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. Consequently, 247.5 GB is about 230.5 GiB. These are two unit labels for the same number of bytes, not evidence that files disappeared.

If a file manager reports GiB, use the unit-conversion field before entering capacity numbers. If its label is ambiguous, prefer an exact byte count or the operating system’s documentation. Mixing a decimal budget with a binary free-space reading can produce a false shortage or surplus.

Replace the estimate with observations

Write down the collection size and the date at two comparable points. Net additions divided by elapsed months give a starting growth estimate. A month with an overseas trip or a video project may not represent the rest of the year; test a higher-growth scenario separately.

Revisit the plan after changing camera quality, adding RAW files, keeping edited copies or changing retention settings. A plan can be arithmetically correct and operationally wrong if those assumptions change. Space is only one part of a backup: finish by checking copy integrity and whether you can actually retrieve the files.

item.title: A non-destructive photo recovery drill you can repeat
item.description:
A non-destructive photo recovery drill you can repeat

Test retrieval, not your luck

A backup routine ends with an observation: the copied material can be retrieved and used. This drill is designed to produce that observation without wiping a device, emptying a trash folder or disconnecting an account. It is a planning method developed for this site, not a claim that KYD has tested your hardware or cloud subscription.

Set aside a short, uninterrupted session. Use a small sample first, retain the originals, and create a new destination folder that is not part of your photo synchronization. Do not change live retention settings to perform the exercise.

Choose a sample that can reveal different failures

SampleReason to include itObservation to record
Recent photoExposes a stalled or incomplete recent upload.Correct image, expected dimensions and usable export.
Older imported photoChallenges the assumption that every folder was included.Found by date or known context, not only by a thumbnail.
VideoAdds a playback and sound check.Beginning, middle and end play; expected audio is present.
Special format you useA still JPEG may omit motion, RAW data or an edited version.The components and behavior you actually need survive the export.

This is a targeted sample, not a statistical certificate. Add personally important material that would be costly or impossible to replace. Keep that list private; no one needs to know the contents for you to use the worksheet.

Run the drill without deleting the source

  1. State the route. For example: “Retrieve an exported copy from the external drive into a new test folder.” Do not just write “backup works.”
  2. Retrieve. Copy the sample out of the backup location. Use the provider’s documented export route for cloud material. Note the account or device dependency privately without recording credentials.
  3. Open locally. After retrieval completes, open the downloaded files from the test folder, not from a link in the cloud app. If testing offline access, disconnect only after downloads finish and only if doing so will not interrupt other work.
  4. Inspect. Check content, dimensions, video playback and special-format components. For a plain, unmodified file copy within the 32 MiB limit, also use the local byte comparison.
  5. Record and retain. Keep a short result, date and next action. Leave the originals and the backup unchanged.

The export route matters. Apple documents separate ways to copy originals and notes limitations for Shared Albums. Google’s folder and item backup checks help identify what entered a cloud library. Neither substitutes for opening your own retrieved sample.

Use a record that separates facts from assumptions

Recovery observation sheet

Date: ____________________   Device / app version: ____________________

Retrieval route (no passwords): __________________________________________

Sample scope and formats: ______________________________________________

Observed result: ☐ Retrieved ☐ Opened ☐ Video checked ☐ Components checked

Still untested: ________________________________________________________

Next action and next check date: ________________________________________

Print this page or use your own private note. A filename can reveal a person, event or location; store the sheet where you would store other private backup records. Do not attach it unredacted to a public issue.

Example record: “October 7: three synthetic test files copied into a separate folder; contents compared. No cloud export, photo decoding or full-library recovery tested.” This is the kind of limited statement a software test can support. It would be misleading to rewrite it as “all photos are safe.”

Stop when a result is ambiguous

  • A sample is missing: identify the missing folder or date range before any cleanup.
  • A file opens only online: establish whether you saved a placeholder, a link or the complete file.
  • A hash differs: check for conversion or editing; do not label the original corrupt from that result alone.
  • A copy needs the same unavailable account: your recovery dependency remains unresolved.
  • The drive disconnects, reports errors or is physically failing: stop repeated experiments and seek appropriate recovery help.

Schedule your own next check after a major library move, export-setting change or new storage device. There is no universal interval that proves safety. The value comes from noticing when your assumptions no longer match the actual retrieval path.

Return to the backup self-check to identify unfinished checks, or to the copy map if the independence of your copies is unclear.
